title: Serving runtime: consolidated architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and runbooks
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Summary:
This consolidated reference documents the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes for recent runtime releases, known issues with workarounds, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical team wiki entry for engineers onboarding to the serving runtime, SREs responding to incidents, and benchmarking/optimisation efforts.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: runtime control plane and data plane (request routing, batching, KV cache, kernel selection), the kernel scheduler, profiler and trace tooling, benchmark harness, and operational runbooks.
- Audience: serving-runtime engineers, infra/SRE, performance engineers, model-onboarding, and RD teams running experiments on inference economics.

Quick links:
- CI benchmarking pipeline: infra/benchmarks/serving-bench-runner
- Profiling tooling: tools/runtime-profiler and tools/gpu-inspect
- Release notes: docs/releases/serving-runtime/2026
- Incident runbooks: runbooks/serve-p99-spike and runbooks/node-oom

1) Architecture overview
- High-level: The serving runtime is composed of three logical layers: the Control Plane (routing, decisioning, rollout, config), the Orchestration Layer (node placement, autoscale, capacity pools), and the Data Plane / Inference Engine (kernel execution, KV cache, batching).
- Goals: predictable latency, cost-efficient throughput, graceful degradation and automated fallback to compatible model variants.
- Key components and responsibilities:
  - Router service (routerd): per-tenant routing policies, model variant selection, and fallback logic. SLO: route decision time < 5ms P90. Owner: routing-team.
  - Autoscaler (scale-coordinator): maintains reserved pools for Dedicated, uses burst policies to request spot capacity. Configurable policies per customer. Owner: infra-autoscale.
  - Runtime worker (runtime-worker): GPU process that hosts model shards, manages KV cache, performs kernel selection and kernel scheduling. Exposes local metrics and profiling hooks. Owner: serving-runtime.
  - KV cache service (kv-proxy): optional local-tiered cache for prefix caching across requests. Reduces repeated compute for multi-turn chats.

Design principles:
- Continuous batching: low-latency bin-packing scheduler combines tokens from concurrent requests to maximize GPU utilization while meeting latency SLOs.
- Kernel selection: runtime picks kernels based on model architecture, quantization profile, sequence length, and hardware characteristics. Kernels are annotated with expected throughput and memory curves.
- Graceful degradation: if a preferred kernel is unavailable or would violate memory SLO, the scheduler falls back to a lower-throughput but safe kernel variant.

2) Kernel scheduling: model to kernel mapping and scheduler policy
- Objectives: maximize throughput (tokens/sec) subject to latency SLOs and memory constraints.
- Scheduler inputs:
  1. Request metadata: model_id, seq_len, batchable (true/false), priority tag.
  2. Node state: free SMs, current GPU memory consumption, active KV cache hit rate.
  3. Kernel catalog: precomputed perf profiles per kernel (throughput, latency per batch size, memory overhead).
- Policy summary (pseudocode):
  1. For incoming request, compute candidate kernels matching model/quantization/hardware.
  2. For each kernel, predict batchable window and expected P95 latency using perf profiles and current node load.
  3. Filter kernels where predicted P99 > request.latency_budget or memory_violation = true.
  4. Rank remaining kernels by cost_score = (tokens_per_sec / estimated_dollar_per_token) * priority_weight.
  5. Select top kernel and enqueue request into batch slot; if batch slot timeout passes (configurable), flush.
- Important knobs and recommended defaults:
  - batch_max_wait_ms: 12 (default for low-latency lanes).
  - batch_size_limit: per-model: default 64 for Llama-7B-class, 16 for Llama-70B-class.
  - kernel_fallback_timeout_ms: 50.
  - cost_weight: 0.7 (tradeoff throughput vs. cost).

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
Purpose: reproduce a performance regression or understand hot-paths in the runtime end-to-end.
Prerequisites:
- Access to the profile cluster or a realistic perf node with identical GPU type.
- Build artifacts with debug symbols and runtime-profiler enabled.
- Sufficient load generator to reproduce steady-state traffic.

Procedure:
1. Baseline metrics:
   - Capture metrics for 10 minutes at current load: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, SM occupancy, KV cache hit rate. Use metrics endpoint: curl -s http://<node>:9000/metrics | jq .
2. Lightweight tracing:
   - Enable x-trace sampling at 1% for 15 minutes: curl -X POST http://routerd/admin/trace -d '{"sample_rate":0.01}'
   - Use traces to identify whether the latency is dominated by pre-scheduling (routerd), scheduling (runtime-worker enqueue/dequeue) or kernel execution.
3. Kernel-level profiling (isolated):
   - Use runtime-profiler: ./tools/runtime-profiler profile --target <node> --model <model> --duration 60s --out /tmp/profile.json
   - Collect GPU metrics: nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o D -d 60 > /tmp/gpu-dmon.csv and nvprof/nvtx markers if supported.
   - If using ROCm, use rocprof or rocTracer equivalents.
4. Flamegraphs and timeline analysis:
   - Convert profile.json to flamegraph: ./tools/runtime-profiler report --in /tmp/profile.json --out /tmp/flame.svg
   - Identify hot kernels (>40% cumulative time) and mismatches between expected and observed batch sizes.
5. Replay and experiment:
   - Re-run specific kernels with microbench scripts: ./benchmarks/kernel-microbench --kernel <name> --batch_sizes 1,4,8,16 --seq 128
   - Compare to catalog perf profiles stored at configs/kernel-catalog.json
6. Mitigation steps (examples):
   - If hot-path is pre-scheduling: increase routerd CPU, reduce route decision hooks, or cache auth decisions.
   - If kernel is slow: switch to alternative kernel variant, or use a quantization profile that enables faster kernels.
   - If batch-timeouts are causing latency spikes: reduce batch_max_wait_ms for the affected lane.

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
- Goals: measure tokens/sec, p95/p99 latency across representative workloads and model sizes, and detect regressions in kernel performance.
- Components:
  - Workloads: short-text generation (seq_len 64), chat-style multi-turn (turns 6, avg seq 256), long-form completion (seq_len 1024).
  - Harness: infra/benchmarks/serving-bench-runner (go binary) that can: spin up a test cluster, deploy model variant, submit requests at target qps, and collect metrics.
  - Baseline datasets: prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/production-like/*
- Benchmark cadence:
  - Nightly: full suite across small (7B), medium (13B), and large (70B) model classes.
  - Per-PR: targeted microbench for changed kernel paths and quantization code.
- Regression detection:
  - CI collects baseline metrics and fails PR if tokens/sec drops > 5% for affected kernel or p99 latency increases by > 10% for a lane marked 'guarded' in configs/perf-guards.yaml.
- Reporting:
  - Benchmark results are stored as JSON artifacts and uploaded to metrics storage. Summary dashboard: dashboards/perf/serving-runtime-bench.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)
- 2026-12-20 (v2026.12.20) - Serving Runtime
  - Added multi-kernel fallback path to prevent OOM on mixed-quant workloads. Reduced failovers by 82% in Canary.
  - Kernel catalog refreshed with new fused attention kernel for LLaMA-13B, improving throughput by ~18% at seq_len 512.
  - Scheduler change: batch_max_wait_ms default lowered from 15 -> 12 for low-latency lanes to reduce tail latency.
  - Fixed: memory leak in kv-proxy that affected long-running conversations.

- 2026-11-15 (v2026.11.15) - Hotfixes
  - Resolved rare deadlock in runtime-worker when preemption occurred during cache refill.
  - Improved diagnostics: added nvtx-like markers in runtime traces for cross-team correlation.

6) Known issues and workarounds (triaged list)
- ISSUE-2026-042 (Symptoms: p99 spikes on multi-tenant nodes with burst traffic)
  - Cause: imperfect isolation in the batcher leading to head-of-line blocking by long-seq requests.
  - Workaround: tag long-seq requests with low-priority lane to force isolation. Short-term mitigation: set per-tenant concurrency limit.
  - Owner: serving-runtime.

- ISSUE-2026-037 (Symptoms: occasional OOM on LLaMA-70B quantized variant)
  - Cause: unexpected memory growth in fused kernel path under seq_len > 1024.
  - Workaround: pin model to fallback kernel variant (kernel_id: q-fused-70b-v2) and set kernel_fallback_timeout_ms to 30.
  - Owner: kernel-team.

- ISSUE-2026-019 (Symptoms: GPU metrics reporting gap when upgrading driver)
  - Workaround: restart runtime-worker and reload metrics exporter; schedule a rolling upgrade with drain windows.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
- Runbook: High p99 latency (runbooks/serve-p99-spike)
  1. Confirm: check dashboard p99 across instances and isolate by model and lane.
  2. Scope: identify whether the spike is global (control plane) or node-local (data plane) using /metrics topology.
  3. Quick mitigations: divert traffic using routerd route rules to a compatible model variant or Dedicated pool.
  4. If node-local: cordon node (k8s: kubectl cordon <node>), increase batch_max_wait_ms temporarily to drain pending work, or reduce batch_max_wait_ms to flush small batches depending on root cause.
  5. Post-incident: collect profile artifacts (runtime logs, /tmp/profile.json, nvprof output), open INCIDENT ticket, and run profiling playbook.

- Runbook: Node OOM (runbooks/node-oom)
  1. Verify OOM: check node logs and runtime-worker stderr for OOM allocation stack.
  2. Evacuate: mark node unschedulable and route new traffic away.
  3. Inspect: dump model allocations (curl http://<node>:9000/debug/allocs) and compare to last known good snapshot.
  4. Workarounds: restart runtime-worker, pin to alternate kernel, or reduce model shard sizes via config: configs/model-shards.yaml.
  5. Permanent fix path: identify kernel memory regression and create PR with memory bounds; add microbench to catch future regressions.

8) Team wiki and ownership matrix
- Owning teams and SLAs:
  - serving-runtime: owner for runtime-worker, kernel catalog, primary incident response. SLA: respond within 15m for Sev2, 5m for Sev1.
  - kernel-team: owner for kernel development and perf characterization. SLA: respond within 1 business day for perf regressions.
  - infra-autoscale: owner for autoscaler and capacity pools.
  - routing-team: owner for routerd and policy rollout.

- Onboarding checklist for new engineers:
  1. Read this consolidated doc and related playbooks.
  2. Run the local dev harness: dev/README.md and run ./tools/runtime-profiler --help.
  3. Shadow on-call for two weeks and perform one scheduled benchmark run.

9) Configuration reference (table)
- Note: presented as a pipe-separated table for quick copy/paste into Confluence tables.
| config_key | default | description | owner |
| batch_max_wait_ms | "12" | Max time (ms) to wait for batch fill in low-latency lane | serving-runtime |
| batch_size_limit | "64" | Model-class default max batch size | serving-runtime |
| kernel_fallback_timeout_ms | "50" | How long to wait before switching kernel fallback | kernel-team |
| cost_weight | "0.7" | Weight applied to cost in kernel ranking | serving-runtime |
| perf_guard_tokens_drop_pct | "5" | CI guard threshold for drop in tokens/sec | perf-eng |

10) Appendix: useful commands and scripts
- Collect metrics (node): curl http://<node>:9000/metrics | jq . > /tmp/node-metrics.json
- Enable sampling traces (routerd): curl -X POST http://routerd/admin/trace -d '{"sample_rate":0.01}'
- Run profiler: ./tools/runtime-profiler profile --target <node> --model <model> --duration 60s --out /tmp/profile.json
- Run microbench: ./benchmarks/kernel-microbench --kernel <name> --batch_sizes 1,4,8,16 --seq 128

Contact and escalation:
- Primary on-call: #oncall-serving-runtime in Slack.
- Pager: oncall team has PagerDuty schedule under "serving-runtime".
- For kernel regressions: ping @kernel-lead and open a Perf-Regression ticket with attached microbench results.
